#3718. Here's our second wave of PS Plus games for November 2026 - and Sony's scrapping its barely used PC app

Death Stranding 2! Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii! Atomfall!

Sony's revealed the second wave of games coming to PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra this month, and there are some genuine big-name attractions, led by Hideo Kojima's futuristic delivery man showstopper Death Stranding 2: On the Beach.

Here's the new games coming PlayStation Plus Extra and Premium in November:

And here are a couple of games coming only to PlayStation Plus Premium in November:

There's a lot to recommend in that list. Death Stranding 2 was one of the standout games of 2025. "A busier, louder, and more emotionally resplendent take on this singular hiking sim," Lewis Gordon wrote in Eurogamer's Death Stranding 2 review.

Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii also shone brightly last year, as ridiculous as it was. "A raucous, absurd spin-off that manages to still feel like a first-rate Yakuza game despite the leftfield setting and delightfully unhinged plot," wrote Matt Elliott in Eurogamer's Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii review.

Meanwhile, Atomfall - Rebellion's quirky British take on a Fallout-like post-apocalyptic idea - was awarded three out of five stars. "If you can get over a difficult start and fancy a lean take on the survival genre, Atomfall delivers an intriguing tale worth discovering," Tom Orry wrote in Eurogamer's Atomfall review. It's presumably been significantly patched and smoothed since then.

The Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake also scored three out of five stars. "Some excellent enhancements make this the ultimate version of Dragon Quest 3, but it could still do more to make it wholly welcoming to newcomers," Daniella Lucas wrote in Eurogamer's Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D review.

We didn't review Hell Let Loose, but the popular World War 2 shooter would go on to amass a serious following and spawn a follow-up game in Hell Let Loose: Vietnam recently, which we did review. "The lavish jungles, rigid command structure, and emphasis on communication make Hell Let Loose: Vietnam a fascinating war simulator when it works. But its many variables can all too easily devolve into a miserable snipe-fest," Rick Lane wrote.

There's plenty to be getting on with, then.

Sony also announced in the PlayStation Blog post it's retiring the PS Plus app on PC from 10th December. Why? Because nobody really uses it.

"With a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4 percent) using the PlayStation Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use," Sony wrote. "As a result, the PlayStation Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available."

Asha Sharma doesn't specifically mention AI in her 25th anniversary message, but I'm pretty sure that's what she's talking about.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a message marking the 25th anniversary of the first Xbox console, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma predicts that the future of gaming will look much like its beginning, "when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays." And even though the term never actually appears in her post, yeah, I'm pretty sure she's talking about AI.

Sharma's message kicks off with a blast from the early days of Microsoft, beginning with a look at Microsoft Adventure, an adaptation of Colossal Cave "that looked more like MS-DOS than an early version of Minecraft," and the first-ever Microsoft staff photo that showcases some absolutely spectacular hair. From there it's a quick trip through Microsoft Flight Simulator, Quake, DirectX, and then in 2001, the original Xbox.

Naturally, there's a tribute to the "generations of employees, studios, developers, and partners" who helped create and grow Xbox, and the people who have played on various generations of consoles over the years.

"Since joining Xbox, I've heard stories of friendships that began over a session and lasted a lifetime, of people who met the person they would marry, and of parents now sharing the games they grew up on with their children," Sharma writes. "I've also heard about people who are no longer with us, and how much those hours spent playing together still mean to those who love them. Ultimately, this is why we exist."

From there, Sharma offers thoughts on the future of Xbox, and this is where I think it gets interesting: After comparing the size and capabilities of the original Microsoft Flight Simulator with the 2024 edition, she continues, "While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically. As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this."

How exactly that change will come about goes unspecified, but my guess? She's talking about AI.

"Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break," Sharma writes.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982."

The explosive rise in the cost of game development is undeniable. The pioneering open-world sci-fi RPG Starflight was literally made by five guys; its distant descendant Mass Effect: Andromeda credits 14 people for working on "audio design" alone. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick summed up the situation quite aptly earlier this year, calling big-budget game development "a high-stakes game for big boys only"; the development budget of the upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6 is being talked about in terms of billions.

Despite Sharma's optimistic presentation, though, I'm not entirely confident that an AI-powered future where one person—or even a few—can do what currently takes hundreds is really a desirable outcome.

Alongside questions of ethics and artistic vision, there are also very pragmatic concerns about the long-term future of the games industry itself. Because really, the embrace of AI—not just at Xbox, but everywhere—is about cutting jobs. Bethesda had nine concept artists working on Starfield: What happens when somebody in an office decides they can get the same job done, pretty much, with two guys hammering out prompts? Maybe even just one? Quarterly profits and shareholder return may go up, but I doubt we'll be saying the same about the quality of the games we play.

Sharma concluded by writing that she believes "the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays." I would argue that small teams are already doing that—the big, billion-dollar blockbusters that have prompted these worries seem far more committed to merely giving us more of what we've already got.

#3715. PlayStation's embattled shooter Fairgames has finally been cancelled, a new report says, as live service push withers away

After years of silence, we finally know the fate of PlayStation's embattled live service game Fairgames. The Haven-developed co-op heist shooter has been cancelled, with the silver lining that the studio is not closing down or laying off staff.

According to a new Bloomberg report, the decision to cancel Fairgames was made following the results of a recent playtest. Sony told staff on Tuesday of the playtest's poor reception and of its decision to end development.

"While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," executives Sean Decker and John Doyle reportedly wrote in an email to staff.

"Combined with challenging market conditions in the PvP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

A PlayStation spokesperson later confirmed that developers at Haven will now support other teams within the PlayStation Studios group, as they continue to "explore new creative opportunities".

Fairgames was initially announced in 2023 as one of several in-development live service games, as part of an initiative by former PlayStation boss Jim Ryan to create more than a dozen games that generate recurring revenue.

Most of those titles were cancelled before they were even revealed, and those that made it out, such as Concord, flopped severely. Even Sony darling Guerrilla Games seemingly can't make it work, with recent reports saying the studio's Horizon Hunters Gathering - initially envisioned as a live service spin on the robo dinosaur series - will now shift into a more traditional co-op structure without live service elements. That's assuming the team can show a revamped version of the game to executives by December.

The news of Fairgames' cancellation isn't surprising. The game has had a tumultuous development journey ever since its reveal. Initially set for release in 2025, the game was soon pushed back to 2026, following the departure of studio founder Jade Raymond.

Though Sony later reiterated its commitment to its remaining in-development live service titles, Fairgames was never shown to the public again. That same year, game director Daniel Drapeau left Haven - another key departure suggesting the game had difficulties and might not see release.

Throughout that time, Fairgames has reportedly been reworked multiple times, with a plan for it to be re-revealed under a new name. That name is believed to be Break In, linked to a trademark Sony filed in May, but with the project cancelled, we may never know if that was the case.

As excited as many were to see Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik advance to Dancing With The Stars' semifinals round on the 2026 TV schedule, it came at a cost. Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy were sent home after seemingly being shoo-ins to make the finale. Val is obviously disappointed, but luckily his 3-year-old son knew just what to say to get his spirits up.

Val shared a video on Instagram of his son, Rome, giving him some words of encouragement after his elimination on DWTS. The clip picked up in the middle of a conversation about what happened, and my heart is so full listening to Rome offer his dad words of encouragement:

Yeah, you try your best...if you don't win sometimes. You try to win so many times. People want you to win because you're a great dancer.

It's not a candidate for the best film speeches of all time, but as a parent, I know it meant the world to hear. Knowing that, even if Dancing With The Stars fans wanted you to go home, your kid still is in your corner and wants you to be ok, and that is such a great feeling that trumps everything else.

I'm sure Val's elimination is a big topic of discussion in the household, as Rome's mother, Jenna Johnson, is still on Dancing With The Stars with Harry Shum Jr. The duo is far and away the most talented piar in Season 35, but as we saw with Val and Jenna Dewan's elimination, that doesn't guarantee safety. Val better save this video to pass it along to his wife, just in case:

Tatyana Ali's advancement really throws a wrench in what originally seemed like a straightforward finals lineup. Should fans vote her through to the finale, at least one more couple that many expected to make it to the end will be sent home early. I've already made a few guesses on who that could be, but I think it's safe to say no one is safe headed into the semifinals.

Jenna Dewan and Val's journey on Dancing With The Stars Season 35 was a rollercoaster, which was made more chaotic by the pro's suspension after online comments he made toward Carrie Ann Inaba. Whether that played a factor in them being sent home is up for readers to decide, though I think this was just a case of them not having as many fans supporting them as Tatyana and Jan.

Jenna Johnson and Val have a long-running history on the show, and they have very passionate fans. With him out of the competition, I wonder if their supporters will jump on the Harry train, making their win this season even more inevitable. We've seen surprises before on finale night, so I'm not completely ruling out someone winning over him!

Dancing With The Stars continues on ABC and for those with a Disney+ subscription on Tuesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. These next two weeks might be the most exciting episodes of Season 35 yet, so make sure to mark your calendars! #3713. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

GTA 6 required a total of three ratings reviews by South Korea's GCRB—and Cyberleek might have had something to do with it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has been granted an Adults Only rating in South Korea by the country's Game Content Rating Board. But in the weeks preceding that decision, the board had nearly refused to issue the game an age rating—effectively leaving it ineligible for sale in South Korea—due to ratings officials' concerns that GTA 6 might be way too comfortable hanging unprompted hog.

According to GCRB meeting minutes obtained by South Korean outlet Inven (via Kotaku), GTA 6 required a total of three ratings reviews, in which committee members repeatedly debated the presence of what they described as "out-of-context genital nudity"—a perception that seemed to have been informed by the leaked GTA 6 developer build footage circulated by cryptopeddling cornball master criminal, Cyberleek.

The GCRB's initial rating review for GTA 6 took place on September 10, during which committee members argued over whether the game's "out-of-context genital nudity" was grounds for refusal. Previously, the GCRB's rating standards automatically rejected games with exposed genitalia, but those standards were relaxed in 2025 to permit an Adults Only rating for "cases where suggestive bodily exposure is directly and specifically depicted," as long as that depiction didn't extend to graphic sexual acts.

Despite that revision, the committee members arguing to refuse an age rating for GTA 6 said that, while the GCRB had previously permitted "a certain degree of genital exposure where there is narrative justification," they "did not believe genital exposure to this extent falls within acceptable limits."

As the report notes, that first review meeting occurred before the GCRB received a playable GTA 6 build, meaning that the GCRB members' perception of the extent of visible in-game genitalia could have been informed by Cyberleek's leaked footage of an in-game nudist colony—an area that, despite the abundance of human flesh on display, didn't actually entail much sex going on. It was mostly just nude people standing around doing people things.

The GCRB committee members in favor of an Adults Only rating noted as much, saying that "in this game, scenes with heavy exposure are not particularly sexual," while "conversely, in sexual scenes, exposure is limited." The first meeting ended in a 3-3 tie vote, leading the committee to postpone its decision and instead recommend to Rockstar that the game be modified.

The GCRB did eventually receive a playable build of GTA 6 on September 28—just six days before its scheduled second review meeting on October 2. While an initial report from its gameplay researcher indicated that "genital exposure scenes mostly appeared as one-off mission backgrounds and did not lead to sexual interactions," the committee decided to once again postpone its decision simply because the game was too damn huge for it to be confident that it had seen all the relevant cases of penises and/or vulvas in the wild.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

A few on the committee remained skeptical, however: "The basic principle of rating refusal applies when bodily exposure of sexual acts are depicted explicitly or excessively so as to disrupt social order," one GCRB committee member said. "By that standard, the current bodily exposure is sufficiently explicit and excessive."

In its third and final review meeting on October 16, the GCRB—informed in part by the fact that 10 other institutions like the US's ESRB and Europe's PEGI had issued their own ratings—ultimately voted 8-1 in favor of granting GTA 6 an Adults Only rating. Its researchers concluded that, after playing the game more thoroughly, scenes featuring full-frontal nudity didn't allow for any sexual interaction, and that cutscene sequences where protagonists Jason and Lucia did do sex at each other didn't expose any genitalia.

Interestingly, the GCRB researchers also confirmed that they couldn't replicate the ability to fully strip Jason and Lucia of their clothes that was shown in Cyberleek videos, inadvertently confirming that the GTA 6 build that'll be available to the public won't allow players to roam Vice City in the nude. Apologies if you were particularly invested in seeing Jason's dong.

And additional apologies to the one dissenting GCRB member who still voted for refusing an age rating for GTA 6, in part due to their fear that the rating could serve as precedent for other genres, meaning "background genital exposure will frequently appear in future RPGs as a result." I suspect they're going to have a rough time once Divinity comes out.

#3710. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Replicates Notorious Glitch For Infinite Gold Skulltulas

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Want 100 Gold Skulltulas in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, but don’t want to track all of them down? Well, that’s a weird thing to want, but if you’re sure, someone has found a way to make one specific Gold Skulltula regenerate infinitely by replicating a glitch from the original game…with a bit of extra work added. It’s time consuming and roundabout, but it seems to really work!

In the original Ocarina of Time, you could get as many Gold Skulltula Tokens as you wanted by visiting a grotto outside of Hyrule Castle that’s opened by playing the Song of Storms on a plant. Inside, there’s a Gold Skulltula behind a bombable wall that child Link can defeat at a distance with a boomerang, and then use the boomerang again to collect the token. However, if you used the boomerang to collect the token as you exit the room via the flower elevator, you’ll collect the token on your way out, but the Skulltula itself will be there waiting for you if you reenter the grotto, allowing you to collect the token again and again, infinitely, in the same way.

This glitch’s replication was first noted by Reddit use Wrong-Kangaroo-4352 almost a week ago, but without much detail as to how to make it work. A few commenters at the time pointed out that doing the original method as-is wasn’t working for them:

101 gold skulltulas ð byu/Wrong-Kangaroo-4352 inOcarinaOfTime

But then today, Reddit user theletter454 arrived to explain what was going on. They said that they tried to replicate this glitch with the same grotto and steps, but initially thought that it had been patched out, because when they reentered the grotto, the Gold Skulltula was gone. However, when they finished the game, they noticed that they were missing 1% completion, with the Nintendo Switch Online app pointing to an uncollected token in Hyrule Castle. They returned, and sure enough, the Skulltula was back!

Infinitely Regenerating Skulltula Token in Hyrule Castle byu/theletter454 inOcarinaOfTime

What theletter454 has worked out, along with some help from folks in the comments, is that the loading zones need to be completely reset for the Gold Skulltula to reappear. This means doing something like swapping back and forth between adult and child Link, or warping to areas with different loading zones, like Lake Hylia. So while a bit more time-consuming than just leaving and reentering the grotto, the fundamentals of the glitch remain intact. And yes, you can just load up on 100 Skulltulas this way if you’re short some, though the game’s counter won’t let you bring the number above 101.

As one commenter points out, Nintendo developers including Satoru Iwata, when working on the 2011 3DS remake, talked about deliberately leaving in certain bugs from the original, because some of the staff who played the original game thought they were fun and a core part of the experience. It’s entirely possible that the same thought process happened here too, especially given that this glitch is ultimately pretty harmless.

#3709. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3708. Monster Hunter Wilds' upcoming Ascendance expansion may be getting a beta, some curious Steam backend updates suggest

Monster Hunter Wilds's first expansion, Ascendance, is set for release sometime next year. But, judging by some very suspect recent changes to the Wilds beta app on Steam, we may be playing some of the new stuff earlier than we thought.

On Steam, Capcom quietly updated the Monster Hunter Wilds Beta app to now say Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance Beta test. You can see the change log on SteamDB (via PC Gamer), which also shows an updated key art - all signs that point towards an impending beta for Ascendance.

The beta app is the same one those who played the original Wilds beta had in their library. Though the app was removed following the beta's conclusion, because the two share the same ID, the beta should be visible in users' list of played games under the new name. This could mean players won't need to sign up for the supposed Ascendance beta, seemingly only needing to download the new client.

Seeing as Ascendance itself doesn't have a release date, beyond a nebulous 2027 target, it's hard to speculate when Capcom plans to release the beta. Sometime early in 2027 would be a good guess, perhaps alongside a release date announcement.

Capcom has shown off Ascendance on multiple occasions, more recently in Sony's September State of Play, where we got to see a number of the expansion's new features. A few days later at Tokyo Game Show, we got a first look at returning Elder Dragon Teostra, which we can hunt in the expansion.

Capcom is keen for Ascendance to deliver the level of challenge Monster Hunter is known for, following feedback that the launch version of Wilds simply lacked that expected level of difficulty. While post-launch updates have certainly raised the level of challenge, Ascendance looks to be the next step up.

Dancing with the Stars is a wildly popular reality competition show, which puts out big numbers on ABC (and streaming with a Disney+ subscription). While fans are reeling from the most recent episode that saw Tatyana Ali stay and Jenna Dewan surprisingly eliminated, a contestant from last season is speaking out. Namely Boy Meets World icon Danielle Fishel, who shared that she thinks both the judges and the audience judge women more harshly than the male dancers.

I'm watching DWTS for the first time this season, and the most recent elimination proved to me how important the fan votes truly are. In a clip from the podcast Chicks in the Office's Twitter, Fishel spoke about her experience in Season 34. During it, she got honest about the bias she thinks exists for celebrity contestants, offering:

When I was on the show I didn't want to talk too much about how I felt that the women are maybe more harshly criticized. Not only by the judging, but also by the audience.

While I'm relatively new to Dancing with the Stars, I can see what she's saying. For instance, earlier this season Jena Dewan got middling scores despite being a professional dancer. Then there was #liftgate, where judge Carrie Ann Inaba famously criticized Jenna Johnson's choreography, resulting in her husband Val posting a controversial response and getting suspended for a week. I've also felt like Tatyana Ali and Maura Higgins have both gotten harsher scores than they deserved throughout the current season.

Given the importance of the fan votes, any time the judges get down on one contestant, it has the potential to really sway the public. Later in the same clip, Fishel addressed the way she felt like sometimes the judges pile on contestants, and suggested a way she thinks they could make it better. In the actress's words:

Maybe just pick and choose. Like 'If you're gonna tell her she should articulate her arms, I'm gonna say something really positive.' Just to balance it out a little bit.

As Danielle Fishel said, she kept these thoughts to herself while competing on Season 34 last year. Now she feels comfortable opening up, especially as she watches the current season as a fan. The hosts of Chicks in the Office seem to agree with her, going so far as to say that the judges "treat the grown men on the show like they are children." #3706. Take-Two CEO Says Discs Will Become Gaming’s Vinyl: ‘It’s Going To Be A Very Small Part Of The Business’

DiscsGTA 6Physical GamesPlayStationRockstar GamesVinyl

Grand Theft Auto 6 is the first major console game to release without a physical version. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick doesn’t think it’ll be the last. Physical games will hang around, but not in any mass-market sort of way. He says they’ll become closer to the equivalent of vinyl records in music.

âIt may not be the end, but listen, weâve been talking, you and I, for a long time,â he told The Game Business‘ Christopher Dring in a new interview. âI predicted that digital distribution would be well over 90 percent of the business more than 10 years ago. I donât always get it right, but this one I got right. Will there always be some physical business? Yes, in the same way that thereâs still a vinyl business in recorded music. But itâs going to be a very small part of the business.â

Physical music accounted for just over 10 percent of total music revenue in the first half of 2026, according to estimates by theÂ Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). That comes out to $581 million, roughly 80 percent of which was earned through sales of vinyl.

According to Circana, physical game sales in the U.S. last year hit a 30-year low of $1.5 billion. That was about 2.5 percent of the $60.7 billion consumers spent on âvideo game hardware, content, and accessoriesâ in 2025. Physical game sales are already a smaller chunk of overall game spending than vinyl is for music, and that’s before PlayStation game discs go away entirely in 2028. Game discs becoming vinyl would actually be a rosier outlook than where things currently seem to be trending.

We still don’t know how Microsoft will approach physical media with the launch of its Project Helix family of next-gen consoles, and Nintendo has confirmed it has no plans to abandon physical games during the Switch 2 era, even if it’s already taken a half-step in that direction with game key cards.

Will GTA 6 ever get a disc version? Vinyl has been a way for music lovers to immortalize their favorite albums. Surely the biggest game launch ever deserves something similar? Zelnick previously shot down rumors that GTA 6 wasn’t coming to disc. He’s now demurred on whether it could get a physical release in the future. That sort of âinformation always comes from our labels,” he told Variety this week, leaving the ball in Rockstar’s court to decide.

GTA 6 is getting a vinyl release for its soundtrack, however. Seem a bit hypocritical? It’s probably less surprising when, as revealed in Take-Two’s latest financials, only 2 percent of its current revenue comes from game discs.

#3705. World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunters have found the MMO's first hidden treasure

World of Warcraft secret hunters are a noble breed, known for scouring the MMO for years for hidden trinkets and treasures. With World of Warcraft: Forever's launch, they've uncovered a quest chain for an especially fancy sword.

Over the past week, members of the WoW Secret Hunters Discord found a quest chain that takes place entirely on the Zephras Isle, meaning you'll need to have access to the Skyborne elves to grab this sword. Navigating the island, you'll need to first pick up an ancient heirloom ring from the starting zone. Simple enough!

Then, you'll need to head to Duskwood to gather the Night Watchman's Torch, a handy light source primarily used to light up areas across the darkened woods near Stormwind. It turns out this torch has uses far beyond this one zone however, as taking it back to the Ruins of Ban'aethal on the Zephras Isle will reward you with a secret quest and the Ancient Hilt.

With the hilt and ring, you then must track down an Ancient Blade from one of several spawn locations on the Zephras Isle. Once you finally track it down, that's the end of part one of this quest chain. You get the sword: Eluvi'ana, which on its own isn't particularly strong, but is speculated to be upgraded later down the line.

You then need to get a corrupted water globe from either Darkshore or the Blackfathom Deeps dungeon depending on your faction, do a fetch quest for a hidden spirit in Ashenvale, then take your hoard of special quest items to a NPC in the new Shen'Dralar zone.

He won't give you the finished sword. Instead he sends you to gather more items from higher-level zones. You'll need to raid a secluded vault in Feralas that you can only see with the Ancient Hilt, dive underwater in Azshara, and kill Highborne Shades in Winterspring. Once you've done all that, you can then cleanse the orb up in Hyjal, speak to the fella back in Shen'Dralar, then shimmy over to the end game Dire Maul dungeon to speak to Prince Tortheldrin about *another* sword.

This is how far the World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunter community has gotten to. It's believed that grinding up the Shen'dralar reputation to Honoured is required for the next step, as Prince Tortheldrin pretty much says as much in his dialogue. So the hunt is still on!

These sorts of secrets make up an important part of any good MMO: the solving of mysteries in these vast digital open worlds. In retail WoW, I have fond memories of the Waist of Time quest chain, which was an arduous and comical grind for a fancy belt during the Battle for Azeroth expansion. This secret sword quest chain may very well evolve into something as legendary as that, at least I hope so!

If you're not already playing it, World of Warcraft: Forever is plenty of fun. A record-breaking number of players are making the journey through Azeroth right now, diving into quests and dungeons new and old.

JBL’s Live 780NC over-ear headphones are down to $139.95 from $249.95, a $110 discount that brings them to their lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, you’re getting a feature-rich pair of wireless headphones with active noise cancellation, high-resolution audio support, and battery life that can last through several days of commuting or work sessions. They’re designed for people who like to wear headphones for hours at a time, too, with adjustable metal sliders and earcups that pivot to fit comfortably around your head. The earcups also fold flat to make them easier to pack, although the included soft pouch offers less protection in a bag than a hard case would.

Sound-wise, its 40mm drivers deliver a wide frequency response of 10Hz to 40kHz, while Bluetooth 6.0 support, LDAC, and LE Audio give you options for high-quality wireless listening with compatible devices. The catch is that the default tuning pushes the bass a little too hard (according to this PCMag review), so you may want to spend some time adjusting the sound through JBL’s app—which includes a 10-band equalizer, preset profiles, personalized sound settings, and virtual spatial audio, letting you tailor the listening experience to your preferences.

You also get Bluetooth multipoint for connecting two devices at once, plus a proximity sensor that pauses playback when you remove the headphones. Physical controls handle power, pairing, and volume, while a touch-sensitive surface lets you manage playback and call up your phone’s voice assistant. As for its battery life, JBL claims up to 80 hours of playback with active noise cancellation turned off, or up to 50 hours with ANC enabled. That should be plenty for long-haul flights, extended workdays, or several commutes between charges, although the noise cancellation itself isn’t quite as effective as what you’ll find on some higher-end competitors. The headphones also lack water and sweat resistance, so they’re not the best choice for workouts or rainy commutes.

Paradox Interactive is getting a new boss: Deputy CEO Mattias Lilja will take over from current CEO Fredrik Wester in January 2027, a move Paradox said "is a natural evolution of how the company is already led."

"My plan was never to be CEO for life. The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company’s journey," Wester said in today's announcement.

"Since I returned as CEO, we’ve streamlined our strategy, rebuilt our pipeline and developed our commercial offering. Mattias has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over. Given his experience and vision, he is exceptionally well positioned to take the company to its next level."

As his statement implies, this is his second tenure as Paradox CEO: He held the position from 2009 to 2018, when he resigned and was replaced by Ebba Ljungerud. But Ljungerud's tenure was rocky, and she resigned in 2021 over "differing views on the company's strategy going forward," at which point Wester returned to the role.

In many ways, Lilja has been calling the CEO shots for a few years now anyway, while Wester's focus has increasingly been on Paradox's "long-term development and goals." And he, like Wester, is also a returnee: He left the company in 2020 after five years in various executive roles, but returned in 2021 along with Wester as "chief of staff." Lilja's LinkedIn profile says his primary duty was to "support the Paradox CEO in leading the executive team, aligning the strategic plan with the day to day operations," and that he would "act as the stand-in for the CEO when needed."

"I approach this role with great humility," Lilja said. "Paradox has a unique DNA that has made us one of the greats in deep and engaging strategy and management games. Now we’re stepping up the pace: we will make further investments in our core business, push the boundaries of our game design, work even more closely with our loyal players, develop more and better tools and services that benefit both modders and players, and continue to sharpen our ways of working and our organisation, with player value in focus."

Reaction among the Paradox community on Reddit seems guarded at this point, which is perhaps understandable given how it went the time the company got a new CEO. PC Gamer's Fraser Brown took a deep dive into that in his 2024 report on "the Dark Age of Paradox Interactive," which includes thoughts from Lilja on the "challenges" of success and what he saw as the future of Paradox.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Even back then, Lilja was clearly helping chart the company's course, and there's also some optimism among Paradox follower in the fact that he seems likely to carry on in Wester's footsteps—and an apparent understanding that Wester has been eyeing the door for a while now anyway.

Lilja will take over as Paradox CEO on January 4, 2027.

#3702. As of this week, PlayStation 5 has surpassed 100 million consoles sold

PlayStation 5 has officially surpassed 100m consoles sold, Sony's updated sales data revealed. The milestone was reached on 10th November, almost exactly six years on from the console's launch.

The figure represents 'sell-in' units, meaning those shipped to retailers, as opposed to 'sell-through' which tracks consoles actually sold to consumers. In other words, the number of PS5s in people's homes is smaller than that 100m.

Nevertheless, this is an impressive achievement, and gets the PS5 ever closer to the PS4's 117m, which it achieved by June 2022. It also means the PS5 has almost matched the original PlayStation in units sold (102.4m). As impressive as the numbers are, historical data shows that PS5 sales have been in decline.

Sony hasn't shied away from discussing that fact in its earnings reports. 2.6m PS5 consoles were sold during the most recent quarter (Q2 of FY2026), well below the 4m sold over the same period the year prior. In fact, Q2 of FY2026 is the lowest second quarter on record in terms of units sold since the PS5's launch.

However, it's also worth noting that, small though it may be, the second quarter's result is higher than the first quarter's 1.6m, the second-lowest of any single quarter since the PS5's launch, beaten only by Q4 of FY2025's 1.5m.

If numbers don't recover in the third and fourth quarters, this may be the PS5's lowest year ever in terms of units sold. Although the second quarter's sales boost can be attributed to the high anticipation of Grand Theft Auto 6, the overall downturn is largely due to the console's higher price; Sony raised the PS5 and PS5 Pro's prices on several occasions since 2020. The company's bottom line, however, hasn't been affected much, as its plan to generate more revenue from its already-engaged audience continues to work.

#3701. Halo: Campaign Evolved’s Next Big Update Will Add A Free Horde Mode

Halo: Campaign Evolved is getting a free update later this year that will add Firefight, the franchise’s popular wave-based horde mode, to the game. It’s likely to be the last bit of Halo content to be developed by what remains of Halo Studios as the series moves under Activision.

Earlier this year, Xbox launched Halo: Campaign Evolved, which is set to be the last major Halo game developed by longtime franchise stewards Halo Studios, formerly 343 Industries. While the remake was fine, the $50 price tag felt high considering it didn’t include any multiplayer deathmatch mode or anything else beyond the campaign and some bonus missions you could play alone or with pals. So when it was reported in October that Firefight was going to be added to Campaign Evolved, fans were hopeful. And now Xbox has confirmed that Firefight is indeed being added to the remake soon.

On November 12, Xbox announced via its official website that Firefight is being added to the remake as part of a free update planned to arrive this winter. Folks going to Halo Fest in December will get a chance to play it early before it’s added to the remake. Firefight in Campaign Evolved will support up to four players, just like the campaign’s co-op mode.

Xbox didn’t share any other details about what to expect, but hopefully this is a classic Firefight experience like what we had in Halo: Reach and Halo 3: ODST, the game that introduced the wave-based horde mode to the series nearly 20 years ago.

The previous report that claimed Firefight was in the works for the remake also reported that Theater Mode was set to be added as part of this free update. However, the report claimed the skeleton crew working on Campaign Evolved’s last big update might not be able to pull all of its plans off before the studio is fully closed up for good. So for now, we don’t know if Theater Mode, letting players look at past gameplay clips via replays, will arrive this winter. But at the very least, a pretty good remake will be even better with the addition of Firefight.

Considering it might be a while until we get a new Halo from Activision, now in charge of the series, this is likely the last bit of new Halo content fans will get for some time.

I didn’t think there was any way Survivor 51 could outcrazy that wild Tribal Council confrontation between Kilby, Lewis, Sharonda, Eric, Cristian and Linnea a few weeks ago where two extra votes were played and they all threatened to draw rocks. Wrong. I was wrong. Last night’s Double Duos twist may have outcrazied that mess, as we got an idol play, two shots in the dark and maybe the weirdest extra vote decision in the history of Survivor. It’s that last part I’m particularly fascinated by, as I’ve watched the episode twice and am still baffled by the decision-making. I’m not the only one either.

Let’s walk through this step by step because there’s a lot going on here. Cristian was picked to go on the journey and earned an extra vote that was only good for that night’s Tribal Council. With all the chaos and uncertainty at Tribal Council, however, he and Carter, who were paired as a duo, decided Cristian should play his shot in the dark to try and earn safety for the pair. If you play your shot in the dark on Survivor, which gives you a 1 in 6 chance of drawing a scroll that keeps you safe, you lose your ability to vote. That meant Cristian couldn’t use the extra vote himself and needed to give it away to someone else.

Cristian has a lot of close allies and is a member of the so-called Salt Alliance, but for unclear reasons, he decided to give the vote to Eric, who is not part of the alliance, during Tribal Council. Now, you might be thinking this is the baffling Tribal Council decision I referenced in the headline, but it’s not. I think it was a weird move, but I sort of understand where Cristian was coming from. He told Eric he was giving him the vote to build trust, and since they do have some history together on a shared pre-merge tribe, he may have thought that was the best way to ensure Eric would vote with them. Personally, I would have just had Carter play the vote, but I can kind of, sort of see where he was coming from.

No, the baffling decision was what Eric then did with that vote. He just put it in his pocket and noped out, despite the fact that he knew it was only good for that night’s Tribal Council. In his voting confessional, he said he didn’t think it needed to be played since he thought they had the numbers on their side. So, he just… didn’t play it and let it expire without ever being used.

I was so confused during my first viewing that I thought I must have misheard the television. Nope. I did not. He just didn’t play it because he thought the votes were already there. Not surprisingly, fans on social media were collectively confused as well. I saw numerous tweets trying to work out the why and even former players calling out his bizarre decision.

Now, to be clear, I’m not saying there’s an obvious play Eric should have made with the extra vote. He could have simply thrown it on Jelly and Dev to solidify that trust with Cristian. He could have thrown a random vote on Mike and Maggie to help protect himself and Thien An in case they caught their own stray vote. Either of those paths would have been perfectly fine, but instead, he did nothing with it and opened himself up to possible problems with Cristian.

Everyone knows how many votes were cast last night. They can all count; so, in theory, Cristian and Carter should be able to figure out that Eric just put the extra vote in his pocket. Maybe they make it a thing. Maybe they don’t. Either way, it seems like a wild gamble to take when the vote has no practical value and at least Cristian and Carter and perhaps more players in that alliance can call him out later if he tries to pretend like it’s a real vote as a leverage move later in the game.

I can’t wait to get a full explanation from Eric whenever he does pregame press about why he didn’t use the extra vote. In a perfect world, we'll even get a confessional about it in the edit next week. Regardless of his reasons though, his decision will go down as yet another example of why this season of Survivor has been the best in a long time, at least so far. The castaways are all over the top and ridiculous. The scheming is incessant, and production has mostly found the right balance between twists and getting out of the way. I can’t wait to see how it all concludes.

#3699. "I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released" - former Tekken director Katsuhiro Harada trashes Microsoft's console in front of senior Xbox staff

Katsuhiro Harada, formerly director on the Tekken series, is known for not pulling his punches. This truth was reinforced recently, as he said he wished the Xbox Series S "wouldn't be released" at a developer panel. All while a member of the Xbox team was in the room.

Per Inven Global, Harada was sitting on a panel at the Console Game Developers Conference 2026 in South Korea. The panel was moderated by former Sony president Shuhei Yoshida, and featured Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee (Stellar Blade), Too Kyo Games CEO Kazutaka Kodaka (Dangenrompa), CD Projekt Red associate game director Paweł Sasko (Cyberpunk 2077), Ludeon Studios CEO Tynan Sylvester (Rimworld), and of course CEO of the newly formed VS Studio Katsuhiro Harada (Tekken).

The panel were asked about the advantages of console development, as well as specific challenges when creating games for certain platforms. Harada led the charge, speaking to the advantages consoles provide for fighting game developers, as the hardware is ideal for tournaments and esports events. Following this, he took an opportunity to speak about a console that drew his ire.

"That said, there's something I really want to say while I have the floor. Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released," Harada said (translations to English via Inven Global). Harada then asked Sasko from the CD Projekt Red team whether he was "upset inside" because of the Xbox Series S.

Sasko proceeded to "burst out laughing" according to Inven Global, before responding: "It constantly throws challenges at us and forces us to optimize our code very cleanly."

Harada followed up with additional thoughts: "You just used a very polite and elegant way to say "Xbox Series S sucks," right? (laughs) Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance. When porting to Switch 2, developers can shift their mindset to 'Switch 2 is a distinct device for Nintendo fans!' But with Xbox, after delivering your absolute best output, it feels like having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child.

"Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking 'Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?'"

Sasko stepped up to offer some perks to the Series S. While he agreed that many players the full technical context behind the Series S' weaknesses, he pointed out that optimisation for weaker hardware like the Series S made games run "significantly better" across all platforms. He even had a Cyberpunk 2077 example, as optimisation work done for the Switch 2 version were applied to all platforms "to great effect". Sasko also pointed to the affordability side of the argument, saying that the cheaper price of the Series S allows for market expansion.

Harada responded: "Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

Here, Shift Up's DongKi Lee ended the topic with some optimism for Microsoft's future consoles: "Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox 'Helix'. From an engineer's standpoint, if you provide us with a dev kit first in Korea as early as possible, we will put in our best efforts to develop for it."

Earlier this year Harada founded Vs Studio with SNK's support, with other veterans from Bandai Namco's Tekken team hopping on board for whatever it's working on. As for the Xbox Helix consoles, in this current hardware environment with bloated costs for RAM and other components, it's reportedly looking a tad expensive. Maybe a Series S equivalent is on the cards?

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3697. Hell Let Loose's original developers' Napoleonic-era extraction game, Hunger, gets December early access release, and an open beta this month

Good Fun Corp, the studio made up of the original developers behind Hell Let Loose, has finally announced a release date for its anticipated next project: Hunger. The extraction shooter-slasher game enters early access on Steam on 3rd December, and there's good news if you're eager to try it out before then.

Hunger's first and only open beta has also been announced, taking place 27th-29th November, the weekend prior to its early access launch. Unlike past tests, this one is available for anyone who requests access on Steam.

Though it may appear as yet another extraction shooter on the surface, Hunger offers more complex and intertwined systems than most. For one, combat has a focus on melee with only a few intentionally clunky firearms available. Though this is a PvPvE game, the vs environment side includes the sort of puzzle-solving, questing and dungeon-raiding typical of RPGs. The game's alternate history, plague-ravaged European setting gives it a grimey, steel-and-mud look few games have.

Beyond the in-match experience, Good Fun's ambitions extend to Hunger's MMO-style progression, its hub area with distinct characters and varied playable classes - all of which can be sampled in the upcoming beta.

Hunger just came off a very successful closed beta, which clearly didn't suffer by kicking off right alongside Modern Warfare 4's DMZ early access. Hunger is currently among Steam's most-wishlisted games, with over 700,000 wishlists, according to the developer.

The launch version includes three large maps, six playable characters, and five Mastery trees with more than 100 Masteries to unlock for your characters. Hunger has only been announced for PC so far, but will presumably arrive on consoles following its early access journey.

#3696. GTA 6 might be censored in Japan, if the game's smaller install size and lack of "strong sexual content" warning is anything to go by

GTA 6 is finally coming out worldwide next week, putting an end to a 13-year wait and at least one popular meme format, but the highly-anticipated game might look a bit different in Japan.

Now that pre-loading is live for the Rockstar Games mammoth, players across the globe can finally download the game and drool over its icon for the next week or so. But pre-orderers in Japan have noticed that GTA 6's file size comes to about 208GB on the PlayStation and Microsoft Stores, versus up to 212GB in other regions.

As reported on by GameSpark and covered by Automaton, the game also received the strictest age rating from the Japanese certification board CERO - "Z" which is recommended for players aged 18 and over - but the listing notably doesn't contain one disclaimer seen in other international ratings.

PEGI and ESRB both warn of the game's "strong sexual content." Curiously, CERO's rating includes no such disclaimer. Together, some fans have taken the lack of "sexual content" disclaimer and smaller file size as signs that GTA 6 might not include some of the risque content we know it'll flaunt elsewhere in the world - based on NSFW leaks and a past rating that already clued us into the fact GTA 6 might be the first GTA to feature full-on sex scenes.

The potential regional censorship isn't too surprising, though, considering how trimmed down GTA 5's Japanese release was at the time. Rockstar had to remove and alter a bunch of GTA 5 scenes to comply with the country's normally strict content guidelines, including Trevor's controversial torture segment and multiple scenes featuring nudity. Baldur's Gate 3, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt and many more have been subject to similar restrictions in the past.

Earlier this week, GTA 6 became the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation and Xbox's history. That's also not a huge surprise, either. The juggernaut game's lavish marketing blitz took over London's Selfridges and Rockstar is even hosting an entire music festival starring a couple A-listers.

#3695. The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Bosses, Ranked From Worst To Best

Each of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Timeâs dungeons is punctuated with a boss, often one that requires you to use whatever item you got in that temple and show the game what youâve learned. Going back to them 28 years after the game first came out does reveal that a lot of them are pretty simple fights, but even if they arenât mechanically demanding, they still each have a menacing vibe that reminds you that, despite the childlike wonder of the Zelda universe, things are dire in the kingdom of Hyrule. We decided to rank them from worst to best, and included a couple of the gameâs memorable mini-bosses for good measure.

All you ever really hear about Dodongo before meeting him is that he likes to eat, so I guess it makes sense that he wouldnât even think twice about eating an explosive over and over. A 3D throwback to a boss from the original Legend of Zelda, he has a one-track mind: Heâs a hungry boy who indiscriminately sucks up whateverâs in front of him. Hope he likes gunpowder. Youâre telling me the Gorons couldnât figure out how to beat this guy? Yâall sell these things in packs of five. â Kenneth Shepard

This is my personal least-favorite boss. I have no idea what its backstory is. Itâs visually unimpressive, and trivially easy to defeat in both the original and the remake. Literally just a little ball. Who cares? âRebekah Valentine

As the first boss in Ocarina of Time (and another boss who first appeared in the original LoZ), Gohma is pretty unremarkable compared to the monsters Link will face as the game goes on, but at least heâs a big olâ creepy crawly that looks like it could have infected a giant tree god and it has a giant red eye thatâs just begging to get shot. Maybe put on a goggle next time you hear Linkâs little boots stomping around, my dude. â Kenneth Shepard

Like most things inside Jabu-Jabu, Bariande is kinda gross to look at. Itâs looks like a growth youâd see in a medical textbook growing on the inside of someone whoâs about to be possessed by a fungus or virus, and defeating it basically requires Link to be a living, tunic-wearing, sword-swinging, boomerang-throwing dose of Pepto-Bismol. All its attacks look like radioactive bodily fluid being slung Linkâs way, and I simply donât like to look at it, so clearly, we must kill it. â Kenneth Shepard

Now weâre talkinâ! I love the pacing of this fight. Entering the room, nothing. Just an ominous mist. Then, as you tentatively explore, a hand rips its way out of the ground. You approach to fight, only for it to grab you and hold you still while the actual monster, a gruesome death blob creature, lurches toward you for an attack. Itâs horrifying! Best part, though: you get to fight it a second time as adult Link, this time knowing whatâs coming, and absolutely thrash it. â Rebekah Valentine

The boss fight with Volvagia, who first appeared in Zelda 2, is a fiery game of whack-a-mole with a dragon that has luxurious locks and performs some of the fiercest hairography in all of Hyrule. Even as itâs dying, it swerves and slides around in the air like itâs in the club dancing to a sick beat. A slay. â Kenneth Shepard

It may not be top of this list, but itâs at the top of my list for being absolutely effed up. This is seemingly the body of someone the Sheikah tortured and killed, its hands chopped off and its head apparently gone too, replaced by a freaky eye thing. Thereâs so much going on in this fight. You need the magic lens(es) to even see whatâs going on, arrows to shoot down the hands when they attack, and the hover boots to keep your footing steady as Bongo Bongo bongos the floor to the rhythm of the music. Stressful, chaotic, and disturbing, this is the perfect fight after the grim connotations of Bottom of the Well and Shadow Temple. â Rebekah Valentine

The sorcerer sisters Kotake and Koume are some of the only bosses Link fights in Ocarina of Time that arenât merely monsters. By the time you actually face them and their contrasting fire and ice magic, youâve had more than enough time to hate their guts for their constant belittling and mocking of you across the past and present of Ocarina of Timeâs story. If the fact that they raised Ganondorf wasnât enough reason to want to wipe their smug faces across the Spirit Temple floor, their constant patronizing gets them there. The actual battle against them is one of the more clever ones in Ocarina of Time, requiring you to use the mirror shield to reflect the spells of one back on the other, as each is vulnerable to her sisterâs powers. Eventually, the two fuse into Twinrova, a super-witch that has all the strengths of both. Unfortunately for them, Twinrova also has their weaknesses, and a well-timed deployment of the Mirror Shield can send their magic back where it came. Even death cannot stop them from bickering, as they float toward the light swearing they will haunt Link one day. â Kenneth Shepard

To this day, Dark Link remains a fantastic example of Nintendo being undefeated at predicting how players will approach even the simplest environments. The pacing this room creates: you enter, pause, crossing to see whatâs on the other side, finding nothing. You turn around confused, and then seeâ¦something, by the treeâ¦ah! What a fantastic surprise in the middle of a grueling dungeon, and a genuinely difficult fight as youâre faced with all your own moves, perfectly timed to counter you. Best of all is when you attack and he just jumps on your sword, mocking you. What a badass. â- Rebekah Valentine

Phantom Ganon may just be a puppet for Ganondorf to control from a safe distance, but itâs one of the most striking examples of the shift in Ocarina of Timeâs tone once Link is all grown up. Heâs already walked through the terrifying streets of the broken-down Castle Town, so thereâs no mistaking that the world of childlike innocence he once knew is gone, but perhaps he can escape it, however briefly, by going back to his childhood home of the Kokiri Forest. But no, Ganondorfâs corruption has taken root and spread throughout the wilds he once knew. Phantom Ganon is just an imitation of the evil Link knows is out there, but itâs no less imposing as it rides Ganondorfâs steed into paintings of withered forests with Ganondorfâs castle looming in the background. Taking down this imposter will not stop Ganondorf, but it feels like the first time since Link has awakened in this post-apocalyptic future that he might be able to win this fight after all, and a harrowing reminder of what will happen if he doesnât. â Kenneth Shepard

After youâve already fought a facsimile of him, Ganondorf has a lot to prove when itâs finally time to take the fight to his doorstep. As you climb to his lair at the top of Hyrule Castle, you hear ominous organ music playing in the background, as if the embodiment of pure evil awaits you. And, it turns out, Ganondorf himself is playing this foreboding piece as he waits for Link to bring him the final piece of the Triforce. Itâs all so theatrical. Ganondorf is certainly one with a flair for the dramatic.Â

The initial fight is relatively straightforward, though it has the added challenge of Navi being unable to give you any insight, so you have to figure it all out yourself. You play a game of fireball tennis once more, with the new wrinkle of having to fire Light Arrows at him to get your slashes and stabs in. At first, he seems to go down pretty easily, and it feels like the Great King of Evil might have been all bark and no bite. Itâs not until he rises from the rubble of Hyrule Castle and his true inner evil comes to the surface as he transforms into Ganon, a pig-like monster wielding two giant blades that towers over Link, that he becomes a true threat. Like most Ocarina of Time boss fights, thereâs a pattern to recognize and a weak point to strike, but the feeling of an incoming cataclysm as you fight in the ruins of the castle and the desecrated Hyrule is rained down upon by a dangerous storm is unmatched, ending the game in a desperate, perilous brawl between the forces of light and darkness. â Kenneth Shepard
